question: What are the two main hormone types found in combined oral contraceptives?
explanation: Combined oral contraceptives contain a blend of synthetic estrogen and progestin to prevent pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T012#GNS226_U6_T012_h1)

question: Why might a breastfeeding mother be given a progestin-only pill instead of a combined pill?

options.A: Minipills taste better for the baby
options.B: Estrogen can decrease the breast milk supply

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Estrogen in combined pills can negatively affect milk production, so we prefer progestin-only options (minipills) to keep breastfeeding going strong.

question: Which type of cancer risk is actually lowered by long-term use of combined oral contraceptives?
explanation: By resting the ovaries and stopping ovulation over time, birth control pills actually help protect against ovarian and endometrial cancers. A nice little bonus benefit!

question: How do oral contraceptives help clients who suffer from terrible menstrual cramps?

options.A: They relax the urinary bladder muscles
options.B: They thin the uterine lining, reducing prostaglandin release
options.C: They stop all hormone production in the body
options.D: They increase the total volume of menstrual flow

explanation: When the uterine lining stays thinner, it makes fewer prostaglandins—the pesky chemicals that cause those painful uterine cramps during your period.

question: Which of these conditions means a client should definitely NOT take combined oral contraceptives?
explanation: Spotting red flags is a key nursing skill! Estrogen increases the risk of blood clots, so a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a strict 'no-go' for combined pills.

question: Why should a 38-year-old client who gets migraines with aura avoid combined oral contraceptives?

options.A: It triggers severe allergic skin rashes on the face
options.B: It will cause her migraines to happen every single day
options.C: It significantly increases her risk of having a stroke
options.D: It stops the migraine medication from working properly

explanation: This is a classic safety rule in pharmacology: migraines with aura, plus estrogen, plus being over 35 multiplies the risk of a dangerous stroke.

question: What vital sign must a nurse always check before a client starts taking combined oral contraceptives?
explanation: Always check the BP! Estrogen can push blood pressure up, so we need a safe baseline reading before handing out that first prescription.

question: A client wants a refill for her birth control, but admits she might already be pregnant. What should you do first?

options.A: Perform a pregnancy test before giving the refill
options.B: Tell her to double her dose for the next week
options.C: Switch her to a progestin-only pill right away
options.D: Refill the prescription immediately without questions

explanation: Safety first! Always rule out an existing pregnancy before continuing hormonal contraceptives to protect both the client and potential pregnancy.

question: How many days of backup contraception are needed when starting oral contraceptives in the middle of a cycle?
explanation: It takes 7 full days of taking the pill consistently to reliably stop ovulation if you don't start on day one of your period. Remind your clients to use a condom during that first week!

question: Why do nurses always stress taking birth control pills at the exact same time every single day?

options.A: It ensures the monthly period starts on a weekend
options.B: It reduces the financial cost of the medication pack
options.C: It maintains steady hormone levels in the bloodstream
options.D: It prevents the client from forgetting to eat meals

explanation: Consistency is key! Taking it at the same time keeps hormone levels steady so breakthrough ovulation doesn't sneak through.

question: What should a client do if she misses one combined pill by more than 12 hours?

options.A: Take three pills at once on the following morning
options.B: Take the missed pill right away and continue the rest as normal
options.C: Throw away the entire packet and wait for her next period
options.D: Stop taking birth control pills for the rest of that month

explanation: Don't panic over one missed pill! Just take the missed one immediately and keep going with the pack as usual. Protection is usually still intact.

question: Which harmless temporary side effect do many clients experience during their first few months on the pill?
explanation: Spotting between periods can be scary for clients, but reassure them it's very normal as the body adjusts to the new hormones in the first few months.

question: In the ACHES warning acronym for oral contraceptives, what does the letter 'C' stand for?
explanation: The ACHES mnemonic is a nursing classic! 'C' stands for chest pain, which can point to serious issues like a blood clot in the lungs.

question: A client on birth control calls complaining of sudden, severe pain and swelling in just one calf. What is your best nursing advice?

options.A: Instruct her to report to the clinic or emergency room immediately
options.B: Tell her to double her birth control dose to stop the pain
options.C: Advise her to elevate her leg and take a warm bath
options.D: Recommend waiting until her scheduled appointment next month

explanation: One-sided leg pain and swelling screams Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). This is a medical emergency—she needs to stop the pill and get evaluated right away!
